query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal treatment that induces the nucleation of coherent nanoscale precipitates along the internal lamellar colony boundaries will simultaneously enhance both the yield strength and the room‐temperature tensile ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys, relative to the untreated lamellar microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries that serve as initiation sites for microcracks under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.intervention: A precisely optimized heat-treatment process (with controlled temperature, duration, and cooling rate) designed to induce the formation of coherent nano-scale precipitates at the colony interfaces.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation conditions using standard mechanical testing; the thermal processing must be tightly controlled to achieve nano-scale precipitate nucleation without coarsening or unwanted phase transformations.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nano-scale precipitates located at the internal colony boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The coherent precipitates enhance interfacial bonding and act as crack deflectors/barriers. This leads to improved load transfer between the alternating lamellar phases and delays the initiation and propagation of microcracks, thereby counterbalancing the typical trade-off between strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated (baseline) lamellar microstructure, the heat-treated alloy should exhibit a higher yield strength, increased uniform elongation, and a delayed onset of microcracking during room-temperature tensile tests.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with unmodified dual-phase lamellar colonies where microcracks initiate along poorly bonded internal boundaries, leading to brittleness under tensile loading.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected only if the heat-treatment parameters (temperature, time, and cooling rate) are within a narrow window that promotes the formation of uniformly distributed, coherent nano-precipitates; deviation outside this window may result in precipitate coarsening or deleterious phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of strength and ductility improvements is uncertain and likely depends on the specific alloy composition and precise processing parameters. Additional work is needed to optimize the treatment for different eutectic high-entropy alloy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens of the same eutectic high-entropy alloy: one set undergoes the optimized heat-treatment designed to produce coherent nano-scale precipitates at the internal boundaries, and the other serves as the unmodified control. Characterize the microstructure using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or atom probe tomography (APT) to confirm the presence and nature of the precipitates, and perform room-temperature tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (TEM/APT) to detect the presence, distribution, and coherence of the nano-scale precipitates at colony interfaces.
Tensile yield strength and uniform elongation measurements.
Onset point of microcrack initiation during tensile deformation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated specimens either do not exhibit coherent nano-scale precipitates at the internal boundaries or if they do not show a statistically significant improvement in both yield strength and tensile ductility (or even show a deterioration) relative to the unmodified baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . frame.system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloys exhibiting dual‐phase lamellar colonies with abundant internal boundaries where microcracking initiates under room-temperature tensile loading.
frame.goal: Simultaneously improve tensile strength and ductility (i.e. delay crack initiation and propagation) at room temperature compared to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
frame.limitation: Conventional processing methods increase strength at the expense of ductility and have not eliminated the brittleness associated with microcrack initiation along internal boundaries.
root_cause_cues: strength at the expense of ductility
constraints: Intervention must be a single processing strategy
Outcomes must be measured during room-temperature tensile deformation
Improvement must be relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline
frame.regime: Room-temperature tensile deformation under standard mechanical testing conditions
prior_attempts: Multiple microstructural-design and processing strategies that enhance strength but reduce ductility
Conventional processing practices that traded ductility for strength gains
frame.understanding: Hypothesis: Introducing a controlled heat-treatment step aimed at engineering the interphase boundaries—by promoting the nucleation of coherent nano-scale precipitates at colony interfaces—will enhance interfacial bonding and act as crack deflectors. This intervention strengthens load transfer and postpones microcrack nucleation, thereby simultaneously enhancing strength and ductility. In comparison with the unmodified lamellar microstructure, it is expected that the treated alloy will exhibit a higher yield strength, delayed crack initiation, and improved uniform elongation during room-temperature tensile tests. The boundary conditions are defined by the precise control of heat-treatment temperature, duration, and cooling rate to ensure the formation of coherent precipitates without coarsening. Prior evidence from studies in nanostructured and precipitation-strengthened alloys supports the notion that well-distributed, coherent precipitates at key interfaces can both impede dislocation motion and arrest crack propagation. An experiment that would falsify this hypothesis is one wherein the application of the heat-treatment fails to produce coherent nano-precipitates or, alternatively, where the treated alloy does not show any improvement in tensile ductility and strength relative to the untreated baseline.
